About: Clausius–Clapeyron slopes of the coexistence curves at the triple point

Source

Concept
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation, dp/dT = L/(TΔV), integrated with a constant latent heat along each of the three coexistence curves of a pure substance.
Serves
Relating the slope of each coexistence curve at the triple point to the latent heat and the volume change of its transition.
On screen
p/pₜ against T/Tₜ on fixed axes (T/Tₜ from 0.6 to 1.6, p/pₜ from 0 to 15), with the sublimation, vaporisation and melting curves meeting at the triple point (1, 1). On the two curves that end in vapour, the vapour is treated as an ideal gas. The critical point is placed at T = 1.40 Tₜ by choice, as the end of the vaporisation curve; a constant-latent-heat model does not produce one. ℓvap is held at 8.5 kBTt, close to that of carbon dioxide.
Controls
ℓfus from 2.0 to 8.0 kBTt in steps of 0.5; Δvfus from −0.060 to +0.060 vₜ in steps of 0.005, passing through exactly zero, where vₜ = kBTt/pₜ is the vapour volume per molecule at the triple point. This Δvfus range is larger than any real solid shows, as the line beneath the plot states.
Readouts
ℓfus, Δvfus, and the slopes dp/dT of the melting, vaporisation and sublimation curves at the triple point, in pₜ/Tₜ.
Inquiry
Five questions, each answered by moving the two sliders and reading the curves and the slopes.
Misconception
Handled only through the answer choices and their feedback; no wrong idea is stated on screen.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit, then checkEach question is answered from a set of choices; the sliders stay live the whole time.
Stable frameBoth axes are fixed, so any change in a curve is a real change, not a rescale.
Operational quantitiesThe slopes at the triple point are read as numbers in pₜ/Tₜ in the line beneath the plot.
Honest magnificationThe volume change on melting is exaggerated, and the line beneath the plot says so.
Nothing drawn for youNo tangent, slope arrow, angle or reference line is painted; features are found by moving the sliders.
Misconceptions as choicesPlausible wrong ideas appear only as answer choices, with feedback once a choice is made.
Formal layer on demandThe derivation lives in The Physics sheet, opened from the header.
The Slopes of a Phase Diagram
Phase diagram of a pure substance
The volume change on melting is exaggerated so that the lean of the melting curve can be seen.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The steep melting curve

Leave both sliders at their starting values, with ℓfus = 4.0 kBTt and Δvfus = +0.050 vₜ, and read the three slopes at the triple point. The melting slope reads 80 pₜ/Tₜ and the vaporisation slope 8.5 pₜ/Tₜ, although the latent heat of fusion is less than half that of vaporisation. Why is the melting curve so much steeper?

2 · More heat or less volume

Starting from ℓfus = 4.0 kBTt and Δvfus = +0.050 vₜ, where the melting slope is 80 pₜ/Tₜ, consider two changes: doubling the latent heat of fusion to 8.0 kBTt, or halving the volume change to +0.025 vₜ. Try each in turn and return to the start between them. Which of the two makes the melting curve steeper?

3 · Through zero volume change

Set ℓfus back to 4.0 kBTt and slide the volume change on melting slowly down from +0.050 vₜ, through zero, to −0.050 vₜ. What happens to the melting curve?

4 · Squeezing at fixed temperature

Keep Δvfus = −0.050 vₜ and ℓfus = 4.0 kBTt. Consider a sample held at T = 0.97 Tₜ and p = 2 pₜ, a little to the left of the melting curve. What happens to it when it is squeezed at this fixed temperature up to p = 10 pₜ?

5 · Raising the latent heat of fusion

Set Δvfus back to +0.050 vₜ and ℓfus to 2.0 kBTt, then raise ℓfus slowly to 8.0 kBTt while watching all three curves near the triple point. Which curves change?

The Slopes of a Phase Diagram

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A coexistence curve marks the pressures and temperatures at which two phases of a substance can live side by side. This sim draws all three curves of one substance from the triple point, and reads out the slope of each there, while you change the properties of melting.

What you'll learn

  • How the slope of a coexistence curve follows from the properties of its transition.
  • How the slopes of the melting, vaporisation and sublimation curves compare, and what each depends on.
  • How the melting curve responds as ℓfus and Δvfus change, including the sign of Δvfus.
  • Which curves share a latent heat.
The set-up: the sim's axes, with the triple point at (1, 1).

What's on screen

  • Three curves, all in one colour and each named: sublimation, vaporisation and melting.
  • Two dots: the triple point, and the critical point, where the vaporisation curve ends, at T = 1.40 Tt by the sim's choice.
  • Zoom inset: the region T/Tt 0.94–1.06 and p/pt 0.6–1.4, magnified.
  • Readouts: ℓfus, Δvfus, and the slope dp/dT of each curve at the triple point, in pt/Tt.
See itLook at the diagram at your current settings. Watch for: three curves leaving the triple point, and three slopes printed in the Readouts panel.
02

03

The slope of a curve is L/(TΔV)

Take a point on a coexistence curve, where the chemical potentials of the two phases are equal, and move a short way along it. They must stay equal, so their changes are equal. With dμ = −s dT + v dp, that gives (s2 − s1) dT = (v2 − v1) dp.

dp/dT = ΔS/ΔV = L / (T ΔV)
Notes (6.8) and (6.9). L = TΔS is the latent heat of the whole sample, and ΔV its change in volume.

Per molecule, ℓ = L/N and Δv = ΔV/N, so the slope is ℓ/(TΔv). At the triple point T = Tt, and the slope is the ratio of ℓ/kBTt to Δv/vt, in pt/Tt. For melting that is ℓfus over Δvfus.

On the two curves that end in vapour, the vapour's volume dwarfs the other phase's, so Δv ≈ vt there. Numerically their slopes are then ℓvap and ℓsub.

See itSet the opening values, ℓfus = 4.0 and Δvfus = +0.050. Watch for: Melting +80, Vaporisation 8.5 and Sublimation 12.5 in the Readouts.
04

Melting is steep because its volume change is small

At the opening setting ℓfus is less than half of ℓvap, yet the melting slope, 4.0/0.050 = 80, is about nine times the vaporisation slope, 8.5. The volume change sits in the denominator: Δvfus = 0.050 vt is twenty times smaller than the vapour's, and 20 × (4.0/8.5) = 9.4.

The two volume changes, drawn to scale at the opening setting.

The notes say it in a sentence: melting absorbs heat and changes the volume only slightly, so ΔV is small and the slope is large. The sim makes Δvfus larger than any real solid's, so a real melting curve is steeper still.

Even the weakest melting the sliders allow, ℓfus = 2.0 with Δvfus = +0.060, gives 33, almost four times 8.5.

See itSet the weakest melting, ℓfus = 2.0 and Δvfus = +0.060. Watch for: Melting +33, still almost four times Vaporisation 8.5.

Only the ratio matters

Taking ℓfus and Δvfus constant along the curve, as the sim does, dp/dT = (ℓfus/Δvfus)/T integrates to p/pt = 1 + (melting slope) × ln(T/Tt). The two settings enter only through their ratio.

So doubling ℓfus and halving Δvfus are the same change: both take 80 to 160, and the two melting curves lie on top of each other.

ℓfusΔvfusmelting slope
4.0+0.05080
8.0+0.050160
4.0+0.025160
2.0+0.02580
See itDouble the latent heat: ℓfus = 8.0, Δvfus = +0.050. Watch for: Melting +160, and the shape of the melting curve.
See itHalve the volume change instead: ℓfus = 4.0, Δvfus = +0.025. Watch for: Melting +160 again, and the same curve as before.
05

The sign of the volume change sets the lean

ℓ and T are positive, so the slope has the sign of Δvfus. If the liquid takes more room than the solid, Δvfus is positive and the curve leans right, as it does for most substances.

As Δvfus shrinks, ℓfus/Δvfus grows without limit, and at Δvfus = 0 the curve stands vertical: T = Tt at every pressure. The readout then says vertical, because the slope is undefined.

Past zero the slope changes sign and the curve leans left. A negative Δvfus means the liquid is denser than the solid, as for water.

ℓfus = 4.0 and three values of Δvfus. The dashed curve is Δvfus = 0.
See itSet Δvfus = 0, keeping your ℓfus. Watch for: the melting curve standing vertical, and Melting reading “vertical”.
See itSet Δvfus = −0.050, keeping your ℓfus. Watch for: the melting curve leaning to the left, and a negative Melting slope.
06

Where it leans left, squeezing melts

Squeezing at a fixed temperature is a vertical move up the diagram. On a right-leaning curve a solid that starts to the left of the curve stays to the left: pressure raises the melting temperature.

On a left-leaning curve the curve sweeps leftwards as p rises and can pass the sample. Take ℓfus = 4.0 and Δvfus = −0.050. A sample at T = 0.97 Tt and p = 2 pt is solid, since the melting temperature there is 0.988 Tt. The curve reaches 0.97 Tt at 3.4 pt, and at 10 pt it has moved on to 0.894 Tt. By then the sample is liquid.

The sample's path, drawn on the left-leaning melting curve. Both axes are cropped to the region of interest.
See itSet ℓfus = 4.0 and Δvfus = −0.050. Watch for: the melting curve running left, to about T/Tt = 0.89 by p/pt = 10.
07

One slider moves two curves

Going from solid straight to gas is melting followed by boiling, so the heats per molecule add: ℓsub = ℓfus + ℓvap. The volume change is again about vt, so the sublimation slope at the triple point is ℓfus + 8.5.

The three heats at the opening setting.

Raise ℓfus from 2.0 to 8.0 and the sublimation slope goes from 10.5 to 16.5. The melting slope ℓfus/Δvfus moves too. The vaporisation curve depends on ℓvap alone and stays put. On the main axes the sublimation curve hardly moves, so use the zoom inset.

See itSet ℓfus = 2.0, keeping your Δvfus. Watch for: Sublimation 10.5 and Vaporisation 8.5 in the Readouts.
See itNow set ℓfus = 8.0. Watch for: Sublimation 16.5 while Vaporisation stays 8.5, and the sublimation curve turning in the zoom inset.
08

Where it matters

  • Water. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so ΔV is negative for melting and the curve leans left. In reality the lean is tiny: the melting temperature falls by only about 0.0075 K per atmosphere.
  • Boiling at altitude. The vaporisation curve rises with temperature, so at lower pressure water boils at a lower temperature (notes, Section 6.1).
  • Most substances. The solid is denser than the liquid, as for carbon dioxide, so the melting curve leans right and pressure raises the melting point.
Go deeper: why the vapour curves bend

With Δv ≈ kBT/p, the slope becomes dp/dT = ℓp/(kBT2), notes (6.10). With ℓ constant, p = pt exp[−(ℓ/kB)(1/T − 1/Tt)], and the slope grows with p. The sim draws the critical point at 1.40 Tt by choice, because a constant-latent-heat model does not produce one.

09

Summary

In one line. The slope of each coexistence curve at the triple point is fixed by two properties of its transition, and the sim lets you set them for melting and reads all three slopes out.

Key points

  • On every curve dp/dT = L/(TΔV); for melting at the triple point that is ℓfus/Δvfus in pt/Tt.
  • The sign of Δvfus sets the lean, and Δvfus = 0 makes the curve vertical.
  • ℓfus enters the melting and sublimation slopes, but not the vaporisation slope.

Common mix-ups

  • “Melting is steep because its latent heat is large.” At the opening setting ℓfus = 4.0 is less than ℓvap = 8.5. The small Δvfus makes the slope large.
  • “A negative volume change just makes the curve less steep.” It reverses the slope, and the curve leans the other way.
  • “Only the melting curve cares about ℓfus.” The sublimation slope is ℓfus + 8.5, so it moves too.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ℓfus = 6.0 and find the Δvfus that gives a melting slope of 120. Check it against the readout.
  • Set Δvfus = −0.025 and step ℓfus from 2.0 to 8.0. Write down each melting slope and compare it with ℓfus/Δvfus.
  • Set Δvfus = +0.005 and ℓfus = 8.0. Read the melting slope, then describe how the curve looks.
